title: How does an enum with an ABSTRACT method (each constant provides its own body, i.e. constant-specific class bodies) implement the Strategy pattern and replace an `if-else`/`switch` on a type — `Operation.PLUS.apply(a,b)` dispatching to the constant's override — and why is this cleaner and exhaustive compared to a switch?
shortTitle: How does an enum with an abstract method implement the Strategy pattern and replace an if-else/switch?

s1_definition.profdef: An enum can declare an abstract method, which forces every constant to supply its own implementation inside a constant-specific class body. Each constant then becomes effectively a small anonymous subclass of the enum with its own behavior. Calling the method on a constant, such as `ChargeType.FLAT.compute(amount)`, dispatches polymorphically to that constant's override. This is the Strategy design pattern expressed as an enum, where the set of strategies is fixed and the compiler guarantees every strategy is implemented.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India charges different fees for different transaction types: a flat fee for an ATM withdrawal, a percentage fee for an international transfer, and zero fee for an internal transfer between Rajesh and Priya. Instead of one big switch statement that decides the fee, imagine each fee type is its own clerk who already knows how to calculate that one fee. When you hand the transaction to the FLAT clerk, it applies the flat rule; hand it to the PERCENT clerk and it applies the percentage rule. Each clerk is a constant with its own behavior, so there is no central if-else deciding who does what.
s1_definition.oneliner: An enum with an abstract method gives each constant its own behavior, turning the enum into a fixed, compiler-checked set of strategies with no switch statement.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An enum can declare an abstract method, which forces every constant to supply its own implementation inside a constant-specific class body. Each constant then becomes effectively a small anonymous subclass of the enum with its own behavior. Calling the method on a constant, such as `ChargeType.FLAT.compute(amount)`, dispatches polymorphically to that constant's override. This is the Strategy design pattern expressed as an enum, where the set of strategies is fixed and the compiler guarantees every strategy is implemented.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India charges different fees for different transaction types: a flat fee for an ATM withdrawal, a percentage fee for an international transfer, and zero fee for an internal transfer between Rajesh and Priya. Instead of one big switch statement that decides the fee, imagine each fee type is its own clerk who already knows how to calculate that one fee. When you hand the transaction to the FLAT clerk, it applies the flat rule; hand it to the PERCENT clerk and it applies the percentage rule. Each clerk is a constant with its own behavior, so there is no central if-else deciding who does what.

**One line to remember:** An enum with an abstract method gives each constant its own behavior, turning the enum into a fixed, compiler-checked set of strategies with no switch statement.

sections.s2_technical:
When you declare a method `abstract` inside an enum, the enum body is no longer allowed to leave it unimplemented for any constant. Each constant must open a brace block, a constant-specific class body, and provide the method. The compiler enforces this, so if you add a new constant and forget to implement the method, the code will not compile. This is the exhaustiveness guarantee that a switch statement does not give you, because a switch happily compiles even if you forget a case and then falls through to a default or returns a wrong value at runtime.

Behind the scenes each constant with a body becomes an anonymous subclass of the enum. So `ChargeType` is abstract-like, and FLAT, PERCENT, and FREE are each instances of a distinct generated subclass that overrides `compute`. When you write `ChargeType.PERCENT.compute(amount)`, the JVM uses dynamic dispatch to run the PERCENT override, exactly like calling an overridden method on a subclass.

This is the Strategy pattern because each constant encapsulates one interchangeable algorithm. The caller does not know or care which concrete strategy runs; it just calls `compute`. For example `BigDecimal fee = type.compute(amount)` works the same no matter which type it is. A classic Strategy pattern needs an interface plus several implementation classes plus a factory to choose one; the enum collapses all of that into a single, readable type where the strategies are named constants.

Compared to a switch, the enum approach is cleaner for three reasons. First, behavior lives next to the data instead of in a faraway switch. Second, adding a new charge type forces you to implement its behavior, so you cannot forget. Third, there is no risk of a missing case silently returning zero fee, which in banking could mean losing real money on every international transfer. A senior point is that enums can also implement an interface, so `ChargeType` could implement a `FeeCalculator` interface, letting non-enum strategies coexist with enum strategies when needed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India computes a fee for every transaction, and the fee rule depends entirely on the transaction type. Originally this was a long switch statement in the payments service. One day a developer added a new UPI transaction type but forgot to add a case to the fee switch, so UPI transactions charged zero fee for a week and the bank silently lost revenue. This is exactly the problem an enum with an abstract method solves, because the compiler refuses to build if a new constant does not implement the fee method, making it impossible to forget.

Problem 2 — The fee logic was duplicated. The same switch appeared in the fee service and again in the statement service, and they drifted out of sync. This is exactly how an enum-as-Strategy helps, because the behavior lives inside each constant in one place, and every service simply calls `type.compute(amount)`, so there is a single source of truth.

In the mini-project we build a fee engine. We define the `ChargeType` enum with an abstract `compute(BigDecimal)` method, and three constants FLAT, PERCENT, and FREE, each with its own body. We define an `Account` class with debit and credit. We define a `FeeService` that, given a transaction type and amount, computes the fee and debits it. The demo charges Rajesh a flat ATM fee and Priya a percentage international-transfer fee, and shows a FREE internal transfer costing nothing. The code demonstrates abstract enum methods, constant-specific bodies, and polymorphic dispatch.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (balance 1000000) charged a FLAT fee on a 5000 ATM withdrawal, Priya (balance 250000) charged a PERCENT fee on a 100000 international transfer, and Rajesh charged a FREE fee on a 30000 internal transfer.

Step 1: At class load the JVM builds three ChargeType singletons, each a distinct anonymous subclass. FLAT overrides compute to return 20.00, PERCENT overrides compute to return 2% of the amount, and FREE overrides compute to return 0.00.

Step 2: FeeService.applyFee runs for Rajesh with type FLAT and amount 5000. The call `type.compute(5000)` dispatches to the FLAT override, ignoring the amount and returning 20.00. The service debits 20.00, so Rajesh's balance becomes 999980.00.

Step 3: FeeService.applyFee runs for Priya with type PERCENT and amount 100000. The call dispatches to the PERCENT override, which multiplies by 0.02 and rounds, returning 2000.00. The service debits 2000.00, so Priya's balance becomes 248000.00.

Step 4: FeeService.applyFee runs for Rajesh with type FREE and amount 30000. The call dispatches to the FREE override, returning 0.00. The debit of zero leaves Rajesh's balance at 999980.00.

Step 5: Each call logs the type, the input amount, the computed fee, and the resulting balance. At no point does any central switch decide the behavior; the constant itself carried the rule.

```text
[INFO] FLAT fee on Rs.5000 = Rs.20.00 | Rajesh balance Rs.999980.00
[INFO] PERCENT fee on Rs.100000 = Rs.2000.00 | Priya balance Rs.248000.00
[INFO] FREE fee on Rs.30000 = Rs.0.00 | Rajesh balance Rs.999980.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When an enum declares an abstract method, the language forces every single constant to provide its own implementation inside what is called a constant-specific class body. Each constant then effectively becomes a small anonymous subclass of the enum with its own behavior, and calling the method on a constant uses normal polymorphic dynamic dispatch to run that constant's override. This is precisely the Strategy design pattern expressed in a compact, type-safe form, where the set of strategies is fixed and named.

In my banking work I use this for fee computation. I define a ChargeType enum with an abstract compute method, and constants like FLAT, PERCENT, and FREE each implement compute their own way. The flat type returns a fixed amount, the percent type multiplies by a rate and rounds with BigDecimal, and the free type returns zero. The payment service simply calls type dot compute on the amount and never needs to know which concrete rule runs.

The reason this is cleaner and safer than a switch comes down to exhaustiveness and locality. A switch statement compiles happily even if you forget a case, and we actually got burned once when a new transaction type was added but its switch case was missed, so it silently charged zero fee and the bank lost revenue. With an abstract enum method the compiler refuses to build until the new constant implements compute, so forgetting is impossible. The behavior also lives right next to the data in one place, instead of being duplicated in several switch statements that drift out of sync.

A classic Strategy implementation needs an interface, several concrete classes, and a factory to pick one, but the enum collapses all of that into one readable type where the strategies are just named constants, and enums can still implement an interface when I need outside strategies to coexist. So my complete answer is that an enum with an abstract method is the Strategy pattern made exhaustive and self-contained: each constant carries its own algorithm, calls dispatch polymorphically, there is no central if-else, and the compiler guarantees I can never add a new type without giving it behavior.
